title: What to Do If It Happens
introduction: In this module, you will learn what to do if you think you have been scammed, from contacting your bank to reporting what happened.

sections.heading: Stop and check what happened
paragraphs: If you think you have responded to a scam, try to stay calm. Stop replying, do not send any more money and do not share any more information, even if you are put under pressure. Think about what you may have shared, such as card details or a password, so you know what to protect next.
tips: It is fine to end a call or stop replying straight away. You do not need to explain yourself to someone you think is a scammer.

sections.heading: Contact your bank or payment provider
paragraphs: If you have sent money, shared banking details or noticed a payment you do not recognise, contact your bank straight away. Use its official app, its website or the number on the back of your card, not a number from a suspicious message. Getting money back is not always possible, but acting quickly gives you the best chance.
tips: Have the date and amount of any suspicious payment ready. If you paid through a payment provider, such as a credit card company or an online payment service, contact them too.

sections.heading: Secure your accounts and devices
paragraphs: If you shared a password, change it as soon as possible on a device you trust, using the official website or app rather than a link. Change it anywhere else you use the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication if you can, and check your accounts for any payments, sign-ins or changes you do not recognise.
tips: If you think your phone or computer has been affected, for example after installing an app a scammer asked you to, ask a trusted technical support provider for help before using it for banking.

sections.heading: Report the scam and get support
paragraphs: Keep a record of messages, payment details and dates before deleting anything. You can report suspected scams, including suspicious messages, calls or adverts, to the police, an official fraud reporting service or the relevant service provider. Find their official contact details yourself rather than using links from suspicious messages. Reporting may not return your money, but it helps protect others.
tips: Scams can happen to anyone, however careful they are. Talking to someone you trust can help you feel less alone and decide what to do next.

quiz.question: You notice a payment from your bank account that you do not recognise. What should you do first?
options: Contact your bank straight away using its official app or the number on the back of your card.
Wait a few weeks to see whether the money is returned on its own.
Call the phone number in a text message that warned you about the payment.
quiz.explanation: Contacting your bank quickly, using contact details you trust, gives it the best chance to protect your account and look into the payment. A number in an unexpected message could belong to a scammer.

quiz.question: You think you may have told a scammer the password for your online banking. What is a sensible next step?
options: Keep using the account as normal and hope nothing happens.
On a device you trust, change the password through the official website or app, and contact your bank.
Click the link in the scammer's message to change your password.
quiz.explanation: Changing your password through the official website or app on a trusted device stops the old password from working. Your bank can also check for unusual activity and help protect your account.
